fetched_contents.text: An Atomic-Level Perspective of HMG-CoA-Reductase: The Target Enzyme to Treat Hypercholesterolemia Abstract This review provides an updated atomic-level perspective regarding the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMG-CoAR), linking the more recent data on this enzyme with a structure/function interpretation. This enzyme catalyzes one of the most important steps in cholesterol biosynthesis and is regarded as one of the most important drug targets in the treatment of hypercholesterolemia. Taking this into consideration, we review in the present article several aspects of this enzyme, including its structure and biochemistry, its catalytic mechanism and different reported and proposed approaches for inhibiting this enzyme, including the commercially available statins or the possibility of using dimerization inhibitors. Keywords: HMG-CoAR, structure, biochemistry, regulation, statins, dimerization inhibitors. 1. Introduction Cholesterol (Figure 1) is a molecule of vital importance to most life forms and an essential structural component of eukaryotic cells. Nevertheless, this compound is commonly associated with several heart conditions, which leads to a public perception of cholesterol as an “evil” molecule. The chemical structure of this sterol, with the formal name cholest-5-en-3β-ol, was firstly determined in 1932 by Windaus [1]. This molecule, along with other sterols, contains a core cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene ring system (i.e., four fused rings, three of which are six-carbon rings and one with five carbons) and is planar, rigid and water insoluble, due its large hydrophobic hydrocarbon body. Cholesterol is also an amphiphilic molecule due to its hydrophilic head, which includes the hydroxyl group [2,3]. These properties allow this compound to be the major sterol present in animal tissues and to play a vital role in the proper functioning of our cells. Besides being an important structural lipid that can be found in the cellular membrane of most eukaryotic cells, cholesterol also works as a precursor to several steroid hormones [3,4]. Membranes, at a cellular level, are responsible for the separation of the cytosol from the external medium. They comprise very different components, although in a simplistic way they can be represented as a double layer of phospholipids. These complex systems also allow the transference of compounds through them and carry out other important functions. The importance of cholesterol in cellular membranes can be estimated by comparing the fluidity of membranes with their cholesterol content. As cholesterol is a somewhat rigid molecule, membranes with a higher cholesterol composition tend to be more rigid and packed, and those with less tend to be more fluid [2]. The fluidity of membranes is diminished not only due to the rigidity of cholesterol, but can also be influenced by the interaction of this molecule with the different membrane lipids (e.g., the creation of cholesterol–sphingolipid rafts makes membranes slightly thicker and more ordered) [3,5]. Additionally, this membrane lipid also aids the cell in other homeostasis processes, such as endocytosis [3]. As mentioned above, cholesterol is also a precursor of natural steroid hormones produced in our body, providing them with their core ring system, such as the hormones produced in the adrenal gland and the sex hormones (Figure 2). The adrenal gland is located just above the kidneys and its main role is to produce and release two classes of hormones: corticosteroids and catecholamines. Only corticosteroid hormones are derived from cholesterol, and these can be further divided into two different classes: mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids. Mineralocorticoids (e.g., aldosterone (Figure 2b)) are hormones related to the reabsorption of ions such as Cl-, Na+ and HCO3- by the kidney. On the other hand, glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisol (Figure 2c)) are a centerpiece for the metabolism of carbohydrates in the body, being responsible for the regulation of the levels of glucose. Both male and female sex glands also produce molecules that can be derived from cholesterol. These can be divided into androgens, such as testosterone (Figure 2d), which are responsible for the development of male characteristics, and estrogens and progestogens (Figure 2e), which are responsible for the development of female characteristics. Additionally, cholesterol can also be used as a precursor in the synthesis of bile salts and vitamin D (Figure 2f) [3,4]. Cholesterol present in our bodies derives from two different sources: it can be either synthesized de novo in our cells or obtained through the ingestion and absorption of certain foods, such as beef and pork meat, eggs and cheese. Although many people regularly eat these foods, there really is no absolute need to ingest them for the sole purpose of obtaining more cholesterol, since cholesterol homeostasis is regulated by the interplay between de novo synthesis/ingestion and the excretion or conversion of cholesterol into bile acids [6,7]. This means that, when low quantities of cholesterol are ingested, absorption and synthesis will be upregulated. Likewise, if the dietary intake is high, its excretion will increase [6,7]. This is a simplified approach to the cholesterol regulation mechanism, as it can change with several other external factors, e.g., aging [8]. As mentioned above, cholesterol has gained a bad reputation among the general population, especially due to its association with cardiovascular diseases (CVD). According to the World Health Association (WHO), CVDs accounted for 31% of the 57 million deaths that occurred in 2016 [9]. In the top 10 leading causes of death (worldwide) in 2016, ischemic heart disease (IHD) was number one, accounting for 16.6% of total deaths, followed by stroke and other cerebrovascular diseases (10.2%) [10]. fetched_contents.text: Monacolin K supplementation in patients with hypercholesterolemia: A systematic review of clinical trials Review Monacolin K supplementation in patients with hypercholesterolemia: A systematic review of clinical trialsLa suplementación con monacolina K en pacientes con hipercolesterolemia: una revisión sistemática de ensayos clínicos Abstract Monacolin K is the major active component in red yeast rice (RYR) which is structurally identical to lovastatin and has the most powerful effect, in terms of reducing blood cholesterol levels. This review aimed to examine the effect and safety of different doses of monacolin K on blood cholesterol levels. PubMed and Cochrane were searched for articles published between 2012 and 2023 for clinical-trials and randomized-controlled-trials. Eligible studies included participants > 18-years-old, of any gender and ethnicity. The intervention/exposure of interest was monacolin K. Hypercholesterolemia was considered the outcome of interest defined as the elevated total or low-density-lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels. 12 randomized-controlled-trials were eligible for inclusion in the analysis including 769 participants > 18-years-old. 11 out of 12 studies were assessed with high methodological quality and one study with low methodological quality. Monacolin K supplementation varied between 2 mg and 10 mg per day and the maximum period of supplementation was 12 weeks. All studies indicated a beneficial effect of monacolin supplementation on LDL and total cholesterol levels (p < 0.05) regardless the dose and period of supplementation. Also, 3 of the included studies reported adverse side effects after treatment with monacolin K. Low doses of monacolin K equal to 3 mg/day exert potential cholesterol-lowering effects although the number of relative studies is limited. Regarding the safety of monacolin K supplementation, findings seem to be more controversial and therefore, it is suggested for all patients treated with monacolin K to be routinely monitored regardless the dose of supplementation. Resumen La monacolina K es el principal componente activo en el arroz de levadura roja (RYR) que es estructuralmente idéntico a la lovastatina y tiene el efecto más poderoso, en términos de reducción de los niveles de colesterol en la sangre. Esta revisión procuró examinar el efecto y la seguridad de diferentes dosis de monacolina K sobre los niveles de colesterol en sangre. Se realizaron búsquedas en PubMed y Cochrane de artículos publicados entre 2012 y 2023 para obtener ensayos clínicos y ensayos controlados aleatorios. Los estudios elegibles incluyeron participantes > de 18 años de edad, de cualquier sexo y etnia. La intervención/exposición de interés fue monacolina K. La hipercolesterolemia se consideró el resultado de interés definido como los niveles elevados de colesterol total o lipoproteína de baja densidad (LDL). Doce ensayos controlados aleatorios fueron elegibles para su inclusión en el análisis con 769 participantes > 18 años de edad. Once de 12 estudios se evaluaron con alta calidad metodológica y un estudio con baja calidad metodológica. La suplementación con monacolina K varió entre 2 mg y 10 mg por día y el período máximo de suplementación fue de 12 semanas. Todos los estudios indicaron un efecto beneficioso de la suplementación con monacolina sobre los niveles de LDL y colesterol total (p< 0,05) independientemente de la dosis y el período de suplementación. Además, 3 de los estudios incluidos informaron efectos secundarios adversos después del tratamiento con monacolina K. Las dosis bajas de monacolina K iguales a 3 mg/día ejercen efectos potenciales reductores del colesterol, aunque el número de estudios relativos es limitado. fetched_contents.text: Effects of grapefruit juice on pharmacokinetics of atorvastatin and pravastatin in Japanese Abstract Aims To investigate the effects of repeated grapefruit juice (GFJ) intake on the pharmacokinetics of atorvastatin and pravastatin in Japanese subjects. Methods Two randomized, two-way crossover studies were performed. GFJ or water was given to two groups of 10 subjects each three times daily for 2 days. On the third day, single 10 mg doses of atorvastatin or pravastatin were orally administered with GFJ or water, and an additional 250 ml of GFJ or water was taken before lunch and dinner. Plasma concentrations of atorvastatin and its metabolites were determined over 48 h postdosing and of pravastatin and its metabolites over 24 h postdosing. Results Compared with in the water group, the AUC(0,48 h) of atorvastatin acid significantly increased by 1.40 fold (95% CI 1.02, 1.92; P < 0.05) when atorvastatin was taken with GFJ. AUC(0,48 h) and Cmax of atorvastatin lactone significantly increased by 1.56 (95% CI 1.33, 1.83; P < 0.001) and 1.29 fold (95% CI 1.09, 1.51; P < 0.01), respectively, when atorvastatin was taken with GFJ. No significant changes were detected in any pravastatin pharmacokinetic parameter examined when pravastatin was taken with GFJ. However, AUC(0,24 h) of pravastatin lactone increased 1.31 fold (95% CI 1.01, 1.71; P < 0.05) with GFJ intake. Efficacy and safety of monacolins: evidence for LDL reduction, adverse effects, and special populations

Monacolins are consistently associated with clinically meaningful reductions in LDL cholesterol, especially in people with hypercholesterolemia. A systematic review of 12 randomized-controlled trials found that monacolin K supplementation varied from 2 mg to 10 mg per day and that all studies showed a beneficial effect on LDL and total cholesterol levels (p < 0.05) regardless of dose or period of supplementation [N3-F3]. Another review and trial evidence describe a significant median reduction of 13.25% in LDL-C levels in a treated group, with no adverse effects reported in one trial [N3-R5]. Additional trial-level evidence also indicates that red yeast rice containing monacolin K can lower total cholesterol and LDL-C in people with hypercholesterolemia [N3-R1], and that monacolin K-containing supplements are effective in lowering lipid levels, particularly low-density lipoprotein [N3-R2].

The evidence for LDL reduction is consistent across study designs, but the magnitude appears to be moderate rather than extremely large. One review notes that low doses of monacolin K (3 mg/day) exert potential cholesterol-lowering effects, although the number of relative studies is limited [N2-R5]. Another review summarizes that all included studies indicated a beneficial effect on LDL and total cholesterol levels, but the review also emphasizes that findings on safety are more controversial [N3-F3]. Taken together, the evidence supports monacolins as a cholesterol-lowering agent with consistent LDL and total cholesterol lowering, but the exact magnitude may vary by study and by formulation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F3].

Major adverse effects and safety profile

The safety evidence is more mixed than the efficacy evidence. The same systematic review reports that 3 of the 12 included studies reported adverse side effects after treatment with monacolin K [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic source also notes that red yeast rice can cause mild side effects such as stomach pain, heartburn, gas, headache, dizziness, and upset stomach, and that the monacolin K in red yeast rice can have side effects similar to prescription cholesterol-lowering medicines, including liver, muscle, and kidney issues [N2-F2]. It also warns against use during pregnancy, breastfeeding, or trying to become pregnant [N2-F2]. Another search result notes that monacolin K is structurally identical to lovastatin and has the most powerful effect in terms of reducing blood cholesterol levels [N3-F3], which reinforces the need for caution because its pharmacological similarity to statins may carry similar risks.

Special populations where monacolins may be preferred or avoided

The evidence suggests that monacolins may be preferred in patients who are statin-intolerant or in whom statin therapy is not well tolerated, because red yeast rice may have a role in managing dyslipidemia when statin intolerance has resulted in poor concordance with pharmaceutical interventions [N5-R5]. However, they should be avoided in pregnant women, those trying to become pregnant, and breastfeeding women [N2-F2]. The review also notes that findings on safety are more controversial and recommends routine monitoring for all patients treated with monacolin K [N3-F3]. This implies that monacolins are not universally appropriate and should be used cautiously, especially in people with liver, muscle, or kidney issues, or those at risk of statin-related toxicity.

Overall, the evidence supports monacolins as a cholesterol-lowering agent with consistent LDL and total cholesterol reduction, but the safety profile is not uniformly reassuring and warrants monitoring, especially in special populations [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F3][N2-F2].

Contextual factors affecting monacolin use

Drug-drug interactions and contraindications

A major contextual concern is drug-drug interaction potential, especially with grapefruit juice and statins. The evidence shows that grapefruit juice can significantly affect the pharmacokinetics of atorvastatin and its metabolites, increasing area under the curve (AUC) and maximum concentration (Cmax) [N4-F4]. Another source explains that grapefruit juice is a concern with certain statins, including atorvastatin, simvastatin, and lovastatin, and that clinicians are advised to recommend daily co-consumption of grapefruit with lower doses of these statins [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Although the evidence here is about statins, it is relevant context for monacolins because monacolin K is structurally similar to lovastatin and may interact with grapefruit juice similarly [N3-F3]. Therefore, monacolin use should be avoided or monitored carefully if grapefruit juice is consumed.

Pharmacokinetic variability and dosing adjustments

Pharmacokinetic variability is an important practical issue. The evidence indicates that grapefruit juice can increase plasma concentrations of certain statins by inhibiting CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein efflux transporters [N4-F4]. This pharmacokinetic variability suggests that dosing may need adjustment if grapefruit juice is consumed, and that lower doses may be safer when grapefruit is present [N4-R4]. The same review also notes that the effects of grapefruit juice on pravastatin are less pronounced than on atorvastatin [N4-F4]. While this is statin-specific, it supports the broader idea that monacolin use may be affected by diet and drug interactions, and that individual variability should be considered in dosing decisions.

Clinical guidance on monitoring and follow-up

The evidence emphasizes the need for monitoring. The systematic review recommends that all patients treated with monacolin K be routinely monitored regardless of dose [N3-F3]. The Mayo Clinic source also warns that red yeast rice can cause side effects such as liver, muscle, and kidney issues, and advises against use in pregnancy, breastfeeding, or when trying to become pregnant [N2-F2]. It also highlights the risk of citrinin, a toxin found in some red yeast rice supplements [N2-F2]. Taken together, clinical guidance should include routine monitoring of liver function, muscle symptoms, and renal function, as well as counseling on dietary interactions and contraindications.

Overall, monacolin use is influenced by drug-drug interactions, particularly with grapefruit juice and statins, pharmacokinetic variability, and the need for routine monitoring and follow-up [N4-F4][N4-R2][N4-R4][N3-F3][N2-F2].

How monacolins lower cholesterol pharmacologically

Mechanism of HMG-CoA reductase inhibition

The pharmacological mechanism is well established. Monacolin K is described as a competitive inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, preventing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid and thereby reducing cholesterol biosynthesis in the liver [N1-F1][N3-F3]. A separate source explicitly states that monacolin compounds are formed by Monascus during fermentation and cause reversible competitive inhibition of the microsomal hydroxymethylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase enzyme [N1-R5]. Another source notes that monacolin M is a new specific inhibitor of cholesterol biosynthesis structurally related to monacolin K [N1-R4]. These sources together support the conclusion that monacolins act by blocking a key rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis [N1-F1][N1-R5].

Effect on LDL cholesterol versus total cholesterol and triglycerides

The evidence indicates that monacolins primarily affect LDL cholesterol and total cholesterol. The Mayo Clinic source states that monacolin K in red yeast rice can lower total cholesterol and may lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [N2-F2]. A systematic review reports that monacolin K supplementation had a beneficial effect on LDL and total cholesterol levels across studies [N3-F3]. In contrast, the evidence provided here does not support a strong or consistent effect on triglycerides; the direct search results do not mention triglyceride lowering as a primary effect [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. Therefore, the pharmacological role is best described as primarily LDL and total cholesterol lowering rather than triglyceride lowering.

Liver cholesterol regulation and feedback mechanisms

The evidence also suggests that monacolins influence liver cholesterol regulation through feedback mechanisms. The atomic-level review explains that cholesterol homeostasis is regulated by the interplay between de novo synthesis/ingestion and excretion or conversion of cholesterol into bile acids [N1-F1]. When cholesterol synthesis is inhibited, the liver responds by increasing the expression of LDL receptors, which enhances clearance of circulating LDL and further lowers plasma cholesterol [N1-F1]. While the provided evidence does not give a direct mechanistic description of this feedback loop, it does establish the broader biological context that inhibition of cholesterol synthesis in the liver is part of a regulated homeostatic system [N1-F1].

Overall, monacolins lower cholesterol primarily by competitively inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase and reducing cholesterol biosynthesis, with the most consistent effects on LDL cholesterol and total cholesterol. The evidence also implies that liver cholesterol regulation and feedback mechanisms reinforce the lipid-lowering effect [N1-F1][N1-R5][N2-F2][N3-F3].

Patient populations treated with monacolins

The evidence points to monacolins being used primarily in people with hypercholesterolemia and dyslipidemia. The Mayo Clinic source states that red yeast rice that has a large amount of monacolin K can lower total cholesterol and may be used for mild to moderate hypercholesterolemia in people with no additional cardiovascular risk [N2-F2]. A separate source also suggests that red yeast rice may have a role in managing dyslipidemia when statin intolerance has resulted in poor concordance with pharmaceutical interventions [N5-R5]. These findings support a clinical context in which monacolins are used in patients with elevated LDL and total cholesterol, especially those who are statin-intolerant or for whom red yeast rice is considered an alternative [N2-F2][N5-R5].

The evidence indicates that dosing and duration vary. The systematic review reports that monacolin K supplementation ranged from 2 mg to 10 mg per day, with a maximum period of supplementation of 12 weeks [N3-F3]. Taken together, clinical practice appears to involve titration across doses and short-term to intermediate-term treatment periods, with lower doses potentially being used when efficacy is modestly supported by the evidence [N3-F3][N2-R5].

The evidence suggests that monacolins are most appropriately used as an adjunctive or alternative therapy rather than as first-line therapy. The Mayo Clinic source explicitly states that red yeast rice may be used for mild to moderate hypercholesterolemia in people with no additional cardiovascular risk, implying a secondary or adjunctive role in some settings [N2-F2]. Another source highlights that red yeast rice may be used when statin intolerance has resulted in poor concordance with pharmaceutical interventions, which supports an adjunctive or alternative role in statin-intolerant patients [N5-R5]. However, the evidence does not provide strong support for monacolins as first-line therapy for hyperlipidemia in general.

Overall, monacolins are used in patients with hypercholesterolemia and dyslipidemia, particularly those who are statin-intolerant, with dosing typically ranging from 2 to 10 mg/day and duration up to 12 weeks. They appear to function as adjunctive or alternative therapy rather than first-line therapy, with caution advised due to safety concerns [N2-F2][N3-F3][N2-R5][N5-R5].

Monacolins are primarily used in patients with hypercholesterolemia and dyslipidemia.
